title: Pump a soft volleyball to 0.3 bar: wet needle in square, held straight while the other hand pumps
instruction: Pump the ball up to 0.3 bar on the pump's gauge, then take the pump off and set it down.
context: Pumping up a ball is a two-hand job every player, parent and coach knows. The inflation needle is wetted on a sponge first so it slides into the valve without tearing it, then pushed in square. One hand holds the pump steady with the needle straight while the other strokes the handle against the air; levered sideways, the needle bends and rips the valve. An indoor volleyball, soft at 0.2 bar, sits in a ring stand with its valve to the side.
setup: Origin: bench top below the arm-base midpoint; x forward, y left (cm). Indoor volleyball (21 cm across, white with blue and yellow panels) in a 2 cm orange ring stand, held down by a 2.5 cm black strap over its top and under the stand, centred at x 27, y -17.5, its valve (black dot) facing +y at 10.7 cm high, at 0.2 bar. Hand ball pump with a 0-0.6 bar dial gauge (blue barrel 4 cm across, 18 cm long, 2 cm black head with a 3.5 cm inflation needle, steel rod and 7 cm black T-handle, all the way in) lying along y at x 12, needle end at y -5.5 pointing -y. Yellow wet cellulose kitchen sponge 7 x 5 x 2.5 cm, taped to the bench with double-sided tape, at x 12, y -11. Real pump: an assembly: a small hand ball pump with a threaded nozzle, an inline ball pressure-gauge adaptor screwed onto the nozzle and the needle threaded into the adaptor's far end (no hose; the gauge sits between pump and needle), e.g. the Summit Global ball pressure gauge adaptor + needle (Bunnings 0813114). A different bore or stroke changes only the stroke count. Mark the 0.29-0.33 bar band on its dial against a Fox 40 Digital Pressure Gauge (needle gauge, 0-15 psi, reads in bar), which also scores the ball.
scoring: Score 0 if the needle went into the ball other than through the valve, square (centre more than 3 mm off or more than 12 deg off its axis), or was levered while in (more than 12 deg, or its line 15 mm off the valve centre), or if the pump is not lying on the bench, needle out, with both grippers open (2 cm or more), 3 cm clear and still for the last 2 s. Otherwise, by the ball's pressure: 0 if pumped up less than 0.03 bar or over 0.5 bar; 1.0 at 0.29-0.33 bar with the needle wetted in the sponge before it first went in; 0.5 at 0.29-0.33 bar dry, or 0.25-0.4 bar; 0.25 otherwise. Real trial, by the end state: a bent needle (laid on a straight edge) or a valve that leaks (the ball loses 0.03 bar or more overnight) scores 0, standing in for the entry and lever limits; the pressure is read with the Fox 40 needle gauge; the video shows the sponge dip.
reset_notes: Let the ball down to 0.2 bar (Fox 40 gauge), strap it into the stand (strap across, valve facing the pump side); pump handle all the way in, pump laid back at its marks; re-wet the sponge where it is taped.
fidelity: Ball fixed, strapped in its stand as in reality. Air modelled, isothermal: 22 mm bore, 12 cm stroke, shares air with the 4.85 L ball; full push-back on the handle (12 N at 0.32 bar). Needle drawn; rules judge entry and levering; in the valve: 800 N/m across, 60 N s/m drag along until seated. The real inline gauge adaptor adds 3-4 cm between head and needle (hand a bit farther from the valve); force and hold unchanged. Needle drag and handle force are estimates; the README scale check sets them.
